title: Growing globe artichokes
subtitle: Architectural perennials that produce edible buds in their second year
excerpt: Globe artichokes are large architectural perennials grown from offsets or seed. They produce edible flower buds from June to August in their second year. Each plant needs 1.5 m of space and full sun, and a well-fed crown will crop reliably for five or more years.
sourceNotes: RHS globe artichoke growing guide (rhs.org.uk). Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), kitchen garden section. USDA cooperative extension notes on artichoke production, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: A side shoot growing from the base of an established globe artichoke plant. Offsets are detached in spring or autumn with a sharp spade, each with a section of root attached, and planted as new plants. They establish faster than seed-grown plants and come true to variety. Dividing the crown every three to four years by removing and replanting offsets keeps the plant vigorous.

content.text: Globe artichokes are large, handsome plants as well as productive ones. The edible part is the immature flower bud; left unpicked, it opens into a large purple thistle. Plants started from seed flower in their second year;
taken from an established plant may produce in the first season if planted in spring. Green Globe Improved, Purple Globe, and Romanesco are reliable UK varieties.

Full sun, well-drained, fertile soil, sheltered from hard frost. Globe artichokes are large: allow 1.5 m between plants. They are marginally hardy in the UK; in colder areas (below -5°C regularly), protect the crowns with straw or fleece in winter. In mild areas, the top growth dies back but the crown overwinters safely.

Sow in modules indoors in February or March at 18°C. Transplant outdoors after the last frost in May. Seed-grown plants show greater variability in head size and quality than offset-grown plants; select and keep the best individuals and discard any that produce poor heads in their second year.

Feed with a balanced fertiliser in spring and then monthly through the growing season. Water deeply during dry periods, particularly in July and August when heads are developing. Cut back the top growth in November to about 30 cm and mulch the crown with compost to protect it through winter. Remove the mulch in March.

Cut the main terminal bud first when the scales are tightly packed and the head feels firm, usually June or July. Cut with 10 cm of stem. Secondary buds lower on the stem develop after the main head is cut; these are smaller. If a bud is left and opens into a flower, the season's production for that stem is over. Continue cutting all buds before they open to extend the cropping period.

items.cause: Hard frost penetrating to the root or waterlogged soil.
items.fix: Mulch heavily in November in exposed areas. Improve drainage if the site holds water in winter. Replace with fresh offsets in spring.

items.symptom: Aphids clustering on the scales of developing buds
items.fix: Knock off with a strong jet of water. Submerge the heads briefly in a bucket of cold water before eating to clear any remaining insects from between the scales.
